related_questions.question: How can you tell when a mole is cancerous?

text_blocks.snippet: A cancerous mole, also known as melanoma, can be identified by changes in its appearance, particularly asymmetry, irregular borders, uneven color, and a large diameter (6mm or more). Additionally, evolving moles, meaning those that change in size, shape, or color, or those that become itchy or bleed, should be examined by a dermatologist.
snippet_highlighted_words: changes in its appearance, particularly asymmetry, irregular borders, uneven color, and a large diameter (6mm or more)

text_blocks.snippet: Key features to watch for (ABCDEs of melanoma):

list.snippet: Asymmetry: One half of the mole does not match the other half.
Border: The edges are irregular, notched, or blurred.
Color: The mole has uneven color, with shades of black, brown, and tan, and may also have areas of white, gray, red, pink, or blue.
Diameter: The mole is larger than 6 millimeters (about 1/4 inch), or is growing.
Evolving: The mole changes in size, shape, or color, or develops new symptoms like itching or bleeding.

list.title: Itching, pain, or tenderness:
list.snippet: These symptoms in a mole or spot can be a warning sign, according to HSC Health, says Aesthetic Dermatology Associates.

list.title: Changes in texture:
list.snippet: A mole that becomes scaly, rough, or develops a hard or lumpy texture could be a warning sign.

list.title: The "Ugly Duckling" Sign:
list.snippet: If a mole looks distinctly different from other moles on your body, it may be a sign of skin cancer and should be checked by a dermatologist, according to Palo Alto Dermatology Institute.
If you notice any of the above changes in a mole.
If a mole is painful, itchy, or bleeding.
If you have a personal or family history of skin cancer.
If you have a history of intense sun exposure, especially as a young person.

related_questions.question: Is a cancerous mole raised or flat?

text_blocks.snippet: Cancerous moles, also known as melanoma, can be either raised or flat, and sometimes a combination of both. While some melanomas are raised and bumpy, others can start as flat, discolored patches that may be slightly raised later. It's important to be aware of the warning signs, including changes in size, shape, color, and texture, as well as asymmetry, irregular borders, and multiple colors within the same mole.
snippet_highlighted_words: can be either raised or flat, and sometimes a combination of both

list.title: Raised (or nodular) melanoma:
list.snippet: These melanomas are often raised, bumpy, or dome-shaped and can grow quickly.

list.title: Flat melanoma:
list.snippet: Some melanomas begin as flat, discolored patches on the skin, similar to a freckle or mole. These can be slightly raised or flat.

list.title: Combination melanoma:
list.snippet: Melanomas can also start as flat, discolored patches and then develop a raised area or nodule.

text_blocks.snippet: Key signs to look for, regardless of whether the mole is raised or flat, include:

list.snippet: Asymmetry: One half of the mole doesn't match the other.
Border: Irregular, notched, or blurred edges.
Color: Uneven color, including shades of brown, black, red, white, or blue.
Diameter: Larger than 6 millimeters (about the size of a pencil eraser).
Evolving: Any change in size, shape, color, or elevation of a mole.

text_blocks.snippet: If you notice any of these changes or have a mole that looks different from your other moles (the "ugly duckling" sign), it's crucial to have it checked by a doctor.

text_blocks.snippet: A mole may be cancerous if it exhibits certain changes, such as asymmetry, irregular borders, uneven color, a diameter larger than 6 millimeters, or if it's evolving in appearance. These changes are often summarized by the "ABCDEs of melanoma". Additionally, moles that are itchy, bleeding, or tender to the touch should be examined by a doctor.
snippet_highlighted_words: asymmetry, irregular borders, uneven color, a diameter larger than 6 millimeters, or if it's evolving in appearance

list.snippet: Asymmetry: One half of the mole doesn't match the other.
Border: The edges of the mole are irregular, notched, or blurred.
Color: The mole has uneven coloration, including shades of black, brown, tan, red, white, or blue.
Diameter: The mole is larger than 6 millimeters (about the size of a pencil eraser).
Evolving: The mole is changing in size, shape, or color, or it's developing new symptoms like itching or bleeding.
Itching, bleeding, or pain: These can be signs of melanoma or other skin cancers.
Changes in sensation: A mole that becomes tender, itchy, or painful should be checked.
New moles: While some new moles are normal, especially in childhood, it's still a good idea to have them checked by a doctor, especially if they appear unusual.
The "Ugly Duckling": This refers to a mole that looks different from your other moles.

text_blocks.snippet: It's important to see a doctor or dermatologist if you notice any of these changes in a mole or if you have any concerns about a mole. Early detection and treatment of skin cancer significantly increases the chances of successful treatment.
